title: Jacob Becomes Israel at Peniel
summary: Returning to face Esau, Jacob sees God’s camp, prays on the covenant promises, sends gifts ahead, and wrestles through the night until the Lord renames him Israel.
historicalContext: Jacob has just parted from Laban at Gilead under a covenant of non-aggression (31:44-55), ending twenty years in Paddan-aram. His road south runs through the hill country east of the Jordan, toward the Jabbok, a perennial stream that cuts a deep canyon westward and joins the Jordan some twenty-five miles north of the Dead Sea. Mahanaim, later a fortified town of Gad on the Manasseh border, lay near this route. Esau has settled far to the south in Seir, the rugged country of Edom, where his descendants would dispossess the Horites (Deuteronomy 2:12); a following of four hundred men marks him as a chieftain with a fighting force. Twenty years earlier he had vowed to kill Jacob (27:41), and Rebekah’s promised message of recall never came (27:45). Jacob’s greeting follows the courteous forms of the period, with “my lord” and “thy servant,” and his gift of over five hundred animals of the kinds that made up pastoral wealth (Job 1:3) is a lavish token of submission.
literaryContext: The chapter is the mirror of Genesis 28. Jacob left the land after angels met him at Bethel, and he returns as angels meet him at Mahanaim; both scenes use the same verb for meeting, the same exclamation “this is,” and the same formula for naming a place. Bethel began at sunset, and Peniel ends at sunrise, so the years in exile are framed as one long night. Within the chapter two key words run like threads. “Camp” links God’s host (v. 2) to Jacob’s two companies (vv. 7-10), and “face” runs from Jacob’s hope to cover Esau’s face with a gift (v. 20) to his cry at Peniel that he has seen God face to face (v. 30). Jacob’s prayer (vv. 9-12) stands between two embassies to Esau, and the night struggle closes the chapter with wordplay among Jacob (Ya‘aqov), Jabbok (Yabboq), and wrestled (vayye’aveq). Chapter 33 then shows the reconciliation for which this night prepared him, and Hosea 12:3-5 reads the struggle as prayer and tears.
themes: God’s unseen hosts around his people
Fear brought to God in covenant prayer
Humility and amends toward a wronged brother
Prevailing with God by clinging in weakness
A new name for a changed man
Seeing God face to face and living

outline.title: God’s Camp at Mahanaim
outline.summary: Angels meet Jacob on the road home, and he names the place for the host of God that surrounds his own company.

outline.title: Messengers, Report, and Fear
outline.summary: Jacob sends a humble greeting to Esau, learns that his brother is coming with four hundred men, and divides his household into two camps.

outline.title: Jacob’s Covenant Prayer
outline.summary: Jacob calls on the God of his fathers, confesses his unworthiness, asks for deliverance, and pleads the promise of a countless seed.

outline.title: The Present and the Crossing
outline.summary: Jacob sends wave after wave of livestock to appease Esau, then brings his family and goods across the Jabbok by night.

outline.title: Wrestling at Peniel
outline.summary: A divine Man wrestles Jacob until dawn, cripples his hip, blesses him with the name Israel, and leaves him limping into the sunrise.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob went on his way.” The short clause closes the long chapter with Laban. Laban has gone back to his place (31:55), and Jacob goes on toward his. The phrase recalls his vow at Bethel, where he asked God to keep him “in this way that I go” (28:20). Twenty years later he is on the return leg of that same road, and God is keeping the promise.

“And the angels of God met him.” Jacob does not seek them out; they come to him. The expression “angels of God” occurs only here and in the Bethel vision (28:12), and the verb for meeting is the same one used when Jacob “lighted upon” Bethel (28:11). The narrator is drawing a line from one scene to the other. When Jacob fled the land, angels ascended and descended above him; now, as he comes back to its borders, angels stand in his path.

The timing matters. Behind him is an angry father-in-law whom God has just restrained (31:24, 29); ahead of him is the brother who had vowed to kill him (27:41). Between those two threats the veil is drawn back for a moment so that Jacob may see what has been true all along. Scripture gives no description of the angels and assigns them no message. Their presence is the message. The psalmist later put it into words: “The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them” (Psalm 34:7). Elisha’s servant learned the same lesson when his eyes were opened to the chariots of fire around Dothan (2 Kings 6:17), and Hebrews describes angels as ministering spirits sent out for those who shall be heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְגְּעוּ־בוֹ (vayyifge‘u-vo) — and they met him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb paga‘ describes coming upon someone, often suddenly and without arrangement. It can carry a hostile sense, “to fall upon” (Judges 8:21; 1 Samuel 22:17), but it can also describe a chance arrival at a place, as when Jacob “lighted upon” Bethel (Genesis 28:11). Here the initiative belongs to the angels. The encounter may have startled Jacob, yet its purpose was assurance.

verses.bibleText: And when Jacob saw them, he said, This is God's host: and he called the name of that place Mahanaim.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when Jacob saw them, he said, This is God’s host.” At Bethel Jacob woke and said, “this is none other but the house of God” (28:17); here he says, “This is God’s camp.” In both places he first interprets what he has seen and then names the spot. Bethel was the house of God at the gate of heaven; Mahanaim is God’s encampment on the road. The word translated “host” is the ordinary term for a camp, whether of travellers, herdsmen, or soldiers. An army is in view. Jacob, travelling with women, children, servants, and flocks, discovers that he is not the only company on that hillside.

“And he called the name of that place Mahanaim,” that is, “two camps.” The dual form invites reflection on what the two camps are. They may be God’s camp and Jacob’s, side by side; they may be two bands of angels, one going before and one following behind; or the name may look forward to verse 7, when Jacob divides his own people into two companies. The narrator seems to enjoy the double sense. Whatever the precise reference, the point is plain: Jacob’s small and vulnerable camp is surrounded by a larger one.

The place name lasted. Mahanaim became a town on the border of Gad and Manasseh (Joshua 13:26, 30) and a Levitical city (Joshua 21:38). Ish-bosheth reigned there after Saul’s death (2 Samuel 2:8), and David took refuge there during Absalom’s revolt (2 Samuel 17:24, 27). Centuries later another fugitive king found shelter where Jacob had once been shown that God guards his people.

The sight did not end Jacob’s fear; the next verses show him alarmed and scheming. Yet the vision was given before the bad news arrived. God often supplies the assurance first and lets the trial follow, so that when fear comes, his people have something to remember.

wordNotes.term: מַחֲנֵה אֱלֹהִים (machaneh ’Elohim) — God’s host
wordNotes.explanation: Machaneh is a camp or encampment, often a military one (Exodus 14:19-20; 1 Samuel 17:1). The same noun returns in verses 7, 8, and 10 for Jacob’s two companies, so that God’s camp and Jacob’s camps are set side by side. In 1 Chronicles 12:22 “the host of God” describes an army of overwhelming size. The place name Machanayim, “Mahanaim,” is the dual form of this word.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother unto the land of Seir, the country of Edom.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother.” The Hebrew word for these messengers is the same as the word for the angels of verse 1. God has sent his messengers to Jacob, and now Jacob sends his own messengers to Esau. The echo invites comparison: heaven’s envoys came to reassure, and Jacob’s go out to test the ground and seek peace.

Esau is “in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.” He had moved south and east into the rugged highlands beyond the Arabah, the territory his descendants would hold (36:8; Deuteronomy 2:12). Each of these names recalls the earlier story. Seir sounds like the Hebrew for “hairy,” Edom like “red,” and “country” is the word for the open field where Esau the hunter roamed (25:25, 27, 30; 27:11). The geography itself reminds Jacob of the brother he cheated.

Jacob did not have to go near Seir to reach Canaan; his road ran west across the Jordan. He chose to make contact anyway. Twenty years had not erased the wrong, and he seems to have understood that he could not settle in the land of promise while the breach with his brother lay open. Jesus taught the same order: leave the gift at the altar and first be reconciled to your brother (Matthew 5:23-24).

wordNotes.term: מַלְאָכִים (mal’akhim) — messengers
wordNotes.explanation: Mal’akh means one who is sent with a message or commission. Context decides whether the sender is human (Numbers 20:14; 1 Samuel 11:3) or divine (Genesis 19:1). The repetition between verse 1 and verse 3 is deliberate. The Greek Old Testament uses angeloi in both places, the word from which “angel” comes.

verses.bibleText: And he commanded them, saying, Thus shall ye speak unto my lord Esau; Thy servant Jacob saith thus, I have sojourned with Laban, and stayed there until now:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob scripts the greeting with care. “Thus shall ye speak unto my lord Esau; Thy servant Jacob saith thus.” The terms are those a vassal used toward a superior, and their direction is striking. Isaac’s stolen blessing had made Jacob lord over his brother: “be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother’s sons bow down to thee” (27:29, 37). Now Jacob calls Esau “my lord” and himself “thy servant.” He does not renounce the covenant promise, which was God’s to fulfil, but he lays down every claim to rank that he had grasped by deceit.

The formula “Thus saith” is the same one prophets used when delivering the word of a king or of God. The messengers are to speak in Jacob’s name, carrying his words exactly, as if Jacob himself were standing before Esau.

“I have sojourned with Laban, and stayed there until now.” Twenty years are compressed into a few words, and the reasons for leaving home are passed over in silence. Jacob does not rehearse the stolen blessing or his flight. The verb “sojourned” describes life as a resident alien, someone living on land that is not his own. Jacob presents himself as a man who has been a guest abroad, not one who has built a power base. The words “until now” offer a quiet explanation of the long silence: he has been away all this time, and this is his first opportunity to make contact.

The humility is real, and it marks a change. Jacob is learning to approach his brother on Esau’s terms. Proverbs observes that a soft answer turns away wrath (Proverbs 15:1), and Jacob’s greeting is built on that principle.

wordNotes.term: גַּרְתִּי (garti) — I have sojourned
wordNotes.explanation: From gur, to dwell as a resident foreigner without the rights of a native. The patriarchs are repeatedly described this way, even in Canaan (Genesis 17:8; 23:4), and Hebrews takes up the theme when it calls them strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Hebrews 11:13). Jacob’s choice of word presents his years with Laban as temporary residence, not settled power.

verses.bibleText: And I have oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants: and I have sent to tell my lord, that I may find grace in thy sight.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And I have oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants.” The list serves two purposes. It tells Esau that Jacob is not coming home destitute to claim a share of Isaac’s estate, and it hints that there is wealth available to make amends. Jacob mentions the ordinary animals and servants but leaves out the camels (v. 15), the most valuable of his possessions. He wants to sound comfortable, not powerful.

The purpose of the whole message is stated at the end: “that I may find grace in thy sight.” This is the language of a petitioner seeking the favour of a superior (Genesis 47:25; Ruth 2:13). The man who once took Esau’s blessing by deception now asks for his brother’s goodwill as a gift. The same phrase will recur in the next chapter when the brothers meet (33:8, 10, 15), and it frames the whole reconciliation. Jacob cannot demand peace; he can only ask for it.

wordNotes.term: לִמְצֹא־חֵן (limtso’-chen) — that I may find grace
wordNotes.explanation: Chen is favour freely shown by one who is under no obligation to show it. “To find grace in the eyes of” someone is a standard idiom for receiving kindness from a superior (Genesis 6:8; 39:4). Its first use in Scripture describes Noah, who found grace in the eyes of the LORD; here Jacob seeks the same kind of undeserved acceptance from a man.

verses.bibleText: And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying, We came to thy brother Esau, and also he cometh to meet thee, and four hundred men with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The messengers come back with a report that is brief and ominous. They found Esau, and “also he cometh to meet thee, and four hundred men with him.” They bring no reply to Jacob’s greeting, no word of welcome, no hint of Esau’s intentions. Only the number.

Four hundred was a substantial force for the time. Abraham had routed the eastern kings with three hundred and eighteen trained men (14:14), and David’s band in his outlaw years numbered about four hundred (1 Samuel 22:2; 25:13). Esau had become a chieftain who lived by the sword, as Isaac had foretold (27:40). The phrase “cometh to meet thee” can describe a friendly welcome or a hostile advance (Numbers 20:18-20); Hebrew narrative often leaves it open, and here the reader shares Jacob’s uncertainty.

It is possible Esau intended to show his strength without deciding in advance how he would use it. The next chapter reveals his embrace, and the reason for the change is left to God’s working. For the moment Jacob knows only that the man who swore to kill him is approaching with an army, and that his own camp has no fighters.

wordNotes.term: הֹלֵךְ לִקְרָאתְךָ (holekh liqra’tekha) — he cometh to meet thee
wordNotes.explanation: Liqra’t, “to meet, toward,” is neutral in itself. It describes a courteous welcome when Rebekah goes out to meet Isaac’s servant (Genesis 24:65) and a battle line when armies advance against each other (1 Samuel 4:1). The participle holekh, “is coming,” shows Esau already on the move. Context alone decides the tone, and verse 6 gives Jacob no context.

verses.bibleText: Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed: and he divided the people that was with him, and the flocks, and herds, and the camels, into two bands;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed.” Two verbs are used, and the first is intensified. Fear names the emotion; distress pictures the squeeze of a man hemmed in with no way out. Jacob has seen God’s host, yet fear rushes in, and Scripture records it without softening. He also has a guilty conscience. The danger ahead of him is the harvest of his own deception, and that knowledge adds weight to the threat.

The word for distress is related to the noun Jeremiah uses for “the time of Jacob’s trouble,” a day of unparalleled anguish from which Jacob’s descendants “shall be saved out of it” (Jeremiah 30:7). Daniel speaks of “a time of trouble, such as never was” at the close of history, when God’s people are delivered (Daniel 12:1). The prophets saw in this night of Jacob’s distress a pattern for the final crisis of God’s people: a time when danger presses from without, sin is remembered within, and the only refuge is God’s mercy laid hold of in prayer.

Jacob responds first with planning. “He divided the people that was with him, and the flocks, and herds, and the camels, into two bands.” The word for “bands” is the same word as “host” in verse 2. God’s camp had met him; now Jacob makes two camps of his own. The plan was sensible. He had no army, could not turn back without breaking his covenant with Laban (31:52), and could not outrun Esau with flocks and small children. Dividing the company was the best way to limit his losses. Prudent action and fearful heart sit side by side, and the next verses will show where he finally turns.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּירָא ... מְאֹד וַיֵּצֶר לוֹ (vayyira’ ... me’od vayyetser lo) — greatly afraid and distressed
wordNotes.explanation: Yare’ is fear; me’od, “greatly,” intensifies it. Yatsar lo means “it was narrow for him,” the feeling of being pressed into a tight place. The same verb describes David at Ziklag when his men spoke of stoning him and he “encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (1 Samuel 30:6). The related noun tsarah, “trouble,” appears in Jeremiah 30:7.

verses.bibleText: And said, If Esau come to the one company, and smite it, then the other company which is left shall escape.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob explains his reasoning: “If Esau come to the one company, and smite it, then the other company which is left shall escape.” It is the arithmetic of a desperate man. He cannot save everyone, so he arranges things so that some might survive. The verb “smite” anticipates bloodshed, and Jacob’s fear in verse 11 makes clear that he expected Esau to spare neither mothers nor children.

The plan reveals both Jacob’s practical shrewdness and its limits. He can divide his camp, but he cannot protect it. Only after he has done everything his own wit can devise does he turn to God in prayer, and the order is instructive. The following verses are the first recorded prayer of Jacob’s life, and they rise out of exactly this sense of helplessness.

The next morning shows how Jacob ranked those he loved. When Esau finally appeared, Jacob placed the handmaids and their children first, Leah and hers next, and Rachel with Joseph last, farthest from danger (33:1-2). The order exposed the favouritism that would later breed envy among his sons (37:3-4). Fear brings to the surface what a man values most, and Jacob’s planning, prudent as it was, could not heal the divisions within his own tents.

wordNotes.term: הַמַּחֲנֶה הַנִּשְׁאָר לִפְלֵיטָה (hammachaneh hannish’ar lifleitah) — the company which is left shall escape
wordNotes.explanation: Nish’ar, “left over, remaining,” belongs to the vocabulary of the remnant, and peleitah means an escaped group or survivors. The two words appear together when Hezekiah speaks of “the remnant that is escaped” of Judah (2 Kings 19:30-31; Isaiah 37:31-32). Jacob’s phrase is practical, but it uses terms the prophets would later apply to the people God preserves through judgment.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said, O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, the LORD which saidst unto me, Return unto thy country, and to thy kindred, and I will deal well with thee:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob said, O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac.” This is the first prayer Jacob is recorded as praying, and the longest prayer in Genesis. At Bethel he had made a vow hedged with conditions (28:20-22); here he simply calls on God. The opening address repeats the words with which the Lord introduced himself at Bethel: “I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac” (28:13). Jacob is not inventing a title. He is giving God back his own self-description and placing himself within the family to whom the promises were made.

Then he adds the covenant name and a quotation: “the LORD which saidst unto me, Return unto thy country, and to thy kindred, and I will deal well with thee.” God had told him to go home (31:3, 13), and Jacob was on the road because God sent him. He reminds the Lord, and himself, that the danger he now faces lies on the path of obedience. That is solid ground for prayer. A man who has wandered off on his own scheme can only ask for mercy; a man who is where God sent him can also plead God’s word.

The promise he quotes, “I will deal well with thee,” paraphrases God’s pledge to be with him (31:3) and draws out its meaning: God’s presence brings good. The verb returns in verse 12, so that the prayer is framed at both ends by God’s promise to do Jacob good.

The prayer follows a pattern found in many psalms of lament: address, confession, petition, and an appeal to God’s promise. It is a prayer of covenant faith. Jacob comes as a servant who has nothing to offer, holding God to what God has said. Such prayer honours God, because it treats his word as trustworthy. Believers in every age are invited to pray in the same way, standing on promises God has made in Christ, in whom they are all “yea” and “Amen” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

wordNotes.term: וְאֵיטִיבָה עִמָּךְ (ve’eitivah ‘immakh) — and I will deal well with thee
wordNotes.explanation: From yatav, “to be good,” in the causative stem: to do good, to treat well. Jacob’s wording interprets the promise of presence in Genesis 31:3 as a promise of active benefit. Moses uses the same verb when he urges Hobab to come with Israel, “for the LORD hath spoken good” concerning them (Numbers 10:29, 32). The verb is repeated, doubled for emphasis, in verse 12.

verses.bibleText: I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and of all the truth, which thou hast shewed unto thy servant; for with my staff I passed over this Jordan; and now I am become two bands.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and of all the truth, which thou hast shewed unto thy servant.” The Hebrew is literally “I am too small for all the mercies.” Jacob, who spent his life grasping, measures himself against God’s kindness and finds that he does not come up to it. The man who bargained at Bethel now confesses that everything he has is undeserved.

“Mercies” is plural: Jacob can count separate acts of steadfast covenant love. God protected him from Laban, gave him wives and children, multiplied his flocks, and spoke to him in dreams. “Truth” is God’s faithfulness, the reliability that makes his promises worth trusting. The same pair of words appeared on the lips of Abraham’s servant when God led him to Rebekah (24:27), and they come together again when the Lord proclaims his name to Moses as “abundant in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). The Gospel of John gathers them in Christ, who came “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Jacob also calls himself “thy servant.” He has just instructed his messengers to call him Esau’s servant (v. 4), and now he takes the same title before God. The two acts of humility belong together. He who bows before God can afford to bow before his brother, and the one who knows he is God’s servant does not need to cling to rank among men.

“For with my staff I passed over this Jordan; and now I am become two bands.” He remembers the crossing twenty years earlier, when he left with nothing but a walking stick, his father’s blessing, and God’s promise. Now he has so much that he has had to split it into two camps, and either one would make him a wealthy man. The contrast is offered as praise. The division forced on him by fear becomes, in prayer, evidence of how far God has brought him.

The confession is the hinge of the prayer. Until a person sees himself as too small for God’s goodness, he will treat God’s gifts as wages or as spoils. Jacob’s words anticipate those of the publican who would not lift up his eyes, and who went home justified (Luke 18:13-14).

wordNotes.term: קָטֹנְתִּי (qatonti) — I am not worthy
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “I am small,” from qatan, “small, insignificant.” With the preposition min it means “too small for” something, a vivid way of confessing unworthiness. David uses the related idea when he marvels that God has brought him so far: “Who am I, O Lord GOD?” and calls God’s promise “a small thing” in his sight (2 Samuel 7:18-19). Gideon describes himself as the least in his father’s house (Judges 6:15).

wordNotes.term: הַחֲסָדִים וְהָאֱמֶת (hachasadim veha’emet) — the mercies and the truth
wordNotes.explanation: Chesed is loyal, covenant kindness, love that goes beyond obligation and holds fast. Its plural here points to many concrete acts of such love. ’Emet is firmness and faithfulness, the quality that makes God dependable. The pair is a frequent combination in the Old Testament (Genesis 24:27; Psalm 25:10; Psalm 89:14) and describes the character God reveals in Exodus 34:6.

verses.bibleText: Deliver me, I pray thee, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau: for I fear him, lest he will come and smite me, and the mother with the children.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The petition itself is short and direct: “Deliver me, I pray thee, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau.” Jacob names the danger twice, first by relationship and then by name. The repetition carries anguish. The threat comes from his own brother, the twin he wronged, and there is no disguising it.

“For I fear him.” Jacob does not pretend to a courage he lacks. He tells God the truth about his feelings, as the psalmists often did: “What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee” (Psalm 56:3). Honest confession of fear is no failure of faith. Faith brings the fear to God instead of hiding it or acting on it alone.

“Lest he will come and smite me, and the mother with the children.” The Hebrew picture is literally “mother upon children,” the image of a mother throwing herself over her little ones to shield them, and being struck down with them. Hosea uses the same phrase for the brutality of war (Hosea 10:14). Jacob fears a massacre that would wipe out his whole family. The danger is not to his wealth but to the line through which the promise was to come.

The verb “deliver” returns at the end of the chapter. After the night struggle, Jacob says that his life “is preserved” (v. 30), using the same root. God answered this prayer, but first he answered Jacob’s deeper need. Before saving him from Esau’s hand, God would save him from himself.

wordNotes.term: הַצִּילֵנִי (hatsileni) — deliver me
wordNotes.explanation: From natsal, “to snatch away, rescue.” It describes pulling someone out of danger or out of an enemy’s grasp (Exodus 18:10; 1 Samuel 17:37). The same root reappears in verse 30, translated “preserved,” forming a link between Jacob’s plea and his testimony after Peniel. The psalmists use it often in their cries for help (Psalm 31:2).

verses.bibleText: And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good, and make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good.” Jacob ends where he began, with God’s word. The phrase doubles the verb of verse 9 for emphasis: “doing good, I will do good to thee.” Jacob takes the promise God spoke and holds it up before him. This is how God’s people have always prayed in crisis. Moses pleaded God’s oath to the patriarchs when Israel had sinned with the golden calf (Exodus 32:13), and Nehemiah reminded God of his word to Moses (Nehemiah 1:8-9).

“And make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.” At Bethel God had compared Jacob’s descendants to the dust of the earth (28:14); “sand of the sea” is the image from God’s oath to Abraham after Moriah (22:17). Jacob blends the two, holding to the sense of the promise. The point of his appeal is clear: if Esau slaughters the mothers and children, how can the promise of a countless seed be kept? God’s own purposes are at stake.

Jacob is not trying to manipulate God by reminding him of what he said. God does not forget. Pleading his promises is a way of resting the full weight of a request on his faithfulness. The person who prays this way stops arguing from his own merits, which in Jacob’s case were thin, and argues instead from God’s character. That is why the prayer moves from “I am not worthy” to “thou saidst.”

wordNotes.term: כְּחוֹל הַיָּם (kechol hayyam) — as the sand of the sea
wordNotes.explanation: A standard biblical image for a number beyond counting, applied to Abraham’s seed (Genesis 22:17), to Israel in Solomon’s day (1 Kings 4:20), and to the people of the restoration (Hosea 1:10). Paul quotes Hosea’s use of it when he speaks of the remnant who will be saved (Romans 9:27).

verses.bibleText: And he lodged there that same night; and took of that which came to his hand a present for Esau his brother;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he lodged there that same night.” After praying, Jacob does not flee or march on. He stays put. The verb “lodged” returns in verse 21, bracketing the account of the gift, and it recalls the night at Bethel when he “tarried there all night” (28:11). Once again a night outside the land will bring Jacob face to face with God.

“And took of that which came to his hand a present for Esau his brother.” Prayer did not make Jacob passive. Having committed the outcome to God, he still did what lay in his power to make peace. Some readers see in the gift a relapse into scheming, as though Jacob were trying to buy his brother off because he did not trust God. The narrative does not condemn him for it, and the gift fits what he had wronged. He had taken Esau’s blessing; now he offers a share of the blessing back. When the brothers meet he will call the gift “my blessing” (33:11). Restitution and prayer are partners here. Zacchaeus showed the same instinct when, received by Jesus, he offered to restore fourfold what he had taken (Luke 19:8).

The word “present” is the term later used for the grain offering brought to God (Leviticus 2:1). In daily life it was the tribute a lesser party paid to a greater, or a gift to secure goodwill. Jacob is approaching Esau as a vassal approaches his lord, with a gift in hand.

wordNotes.term: מִנְחָה (minchah) — a present
wordNotes.explanation: A gift or tribute, often brought by an inferior to a superior to express homage or seek favour (Judges 3:15; 1 Kings 4:21). Jacob’s sons will later carry a minchah to the ruler of Egypt (Genesis 43:11). In worship the same word names Abel’s offering (Genesis 4:4) and the grain offering of the Levitical system. Its use here colours Jacob’s approach to Esau with the language of reverent approach.

verses.bibleText: Two hundred she goats, and twenty he goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The inventory begins with the small livestock: “Two hundred she goats, and twenty he goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams.” The ratio of one male to ten females was a sound breeding proportion, so the gift was a working herd capable of multiplying, not merely animals for slaughter. Jacob had spent twenty years as a master shepherd (31:38-40), and the careful numbers show his skill.

Four hundred and forty animals in these two kinds alone made a generous offering. Esau would later protest that he already had plenty (33:9). The worth of the gift lay less in what it added to his flocks than in what it said: the brother who once took was now giving, freely and at real cost.

wordNotes.term: עִזִּים ... רְחֵלִים (‘izzim ... rechelim) — she goats ... ewes
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Ez is the female goat and rachel the ewe, the same word as the name of Jacob’s beloved wife Rachel (Genesis 29:6). Goats and sheep formed the core of pastoral wealth and supplied milk, wool, hair, and meat (Proverbs 27:26-27).

verses.bibleText: Thirty milch camels with their colts, forty kine, and ten bulls, twenty she asses, and ten foals.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list moves to larger and costlier animals: “Thirty milch camels with their colts, forty kine, and ten bulls, twenty she asses, and ten foals.” Camels were the most valuable item in a herdsman’s estate, and nursing camels with their young were prized for milk and future increase. These were the animals Jacob had not mentioned in his first message (v. 5).

Altogether the gift came to about five hundred and fifty head, a lavish sum that announced how seriously Jacob regarded the wrong he had done. Every animal came out of the two camps Jacob had just described in prayer as the fruit of God’s mercies (v. 10). He was making amends from what God had given him, which is the only treasury any penitent has.

wordNotes.term: גְּמַלִּים מֵינִיקוֹת (gemallim meniqot) — milch camels
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “camels giving suck,” nursing females with their calves. Camels appear in the patriarchs’ wealth from Abraham onward (Genesis 12:16; 24:10). Job’s possessions, before and after his trial, are counted in similar categories of camels, oxen, and she-asses (Job 1:3; 42:12).

verses.bibleText: And he delivered them into the hand of his servants, every drove by themselves; and said unto his servants, Pass over before me, and put a space betwixt drove and drove.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he delivered them into the hand of his servants, every drove by themselves.” Jacob does not send the gift as a single mass. Each kind of animal goes as its own herd, under its own herdsman. “Pass over before me, and put a space betwixt drove and drove.” The gaps were deliberate. Esau would meet one herd, hear the message, and then see another coming, and then another. The effect would build with every arrival, wave after wave of generosity breaking over him before he ever saw his brother.

The arrangement also bought time. A slow procession of herds would delay Esau’s advance and give his anger opportunity to cool. Jacob uses all his practical intelligence, but now in the service of peace instead of advantage.

Proverbs observes that “a man’s gift maketh room for him” (Proverbs 18:16). The saying can describe bribery, but it can also describe the generosity that opens a closed door. Jacob’s gift is of the second kind. It asks for nothing in return except a hearing, and it costs him a large part of his wealth.

wordNotes.term: רֶוַח (revach) — a space
wordNotes.explanation: A rare noun, from a root meaning “to be wide, roomy,” and so an interval or open gap between things. Its only other occurrence is in Mordecai’s warning to Esther, where it means relief, literally breathing room: “then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place” (Esther 4:14). A related verb describes the relief that came to Saul when David played (1 Samuel 16:23).

verses.bibleText: And he commanded the foremost, saying, When Esau my brother meeteth thee, and asketh thee, saying, Whose art thou? and whither goest thou? and whose are these before thee?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob briefs the first herdsman in detail. “When Esau my brother meeteth thee, and asketh thee, saying, Whose art thou? and whither goest thou? and whose are these before thee?” He anticipates three questions, the natural challenges of a chieftain meeting strangers on his road: who is your master, where are you going, and who owns these animals? Each servant was to be ready with the same answer.

The verb “meeteth” is the same one used when the angels met Jacob in verse 1. Jacob had been met by God’s host; now he prepares for the moment when Esau’s host meets his servants. The rehearsed conversation shows how much he expects to turn on first impressions, and how carefully he wants the gift understood as a token of submission and goodwill. The answer in the next verse takes the questions in order: the herds belong to Jacob, they are going to Esau, and they are a present.

wordNotes.term: לְמִי־אַתָּה (lemi-’attah) — whose art thou?
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to whom are you?” A question about allegiance and ownership, asked of servants found away from home. David asks the same of the Egyptian slave he finds abandoned in the field (1 Samuel 30:13), and Boaz asks a similar question about Ruth: “Whose damsel is this?” (Ruth 2:5).

verses.bibleText: Then thou shalt say, They be thy servant Jacob's; it is a present sent unto my lord Esau: and, behold, also he is behind us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The answer is scripted: “They be thy servant Jacob’s; it is a present sent unto my lord Esau.” The words echo the first message (v. 4). Every herdsman is to call Jacob Esau’s servant and Esau Jacob’s lord, so that the message of humility is repeated as often as the gift. The animals belong to Jacob, but they are being given away, and the giving is the point.

“And, behold, also he is behind us.” This last line matters most. The gift is not a substitute for Jacob’s presence or a payment to keep Esau away. Jacob himself is coming. He will not hide behind his herds forever; he intends to stand before his brother face to face. The gift prepares the way for a personal meeting, which is the only way the breach can truly be healed.

wordNotes.term: לְעַבְדְּךָ (le‘avdekha) — thy servant’s
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Eved is a slave or servant, also used in courteous speech as a self-designation before a superior (Genesis 18:3; 44:18). Jacob’s repeated use of the word reverses Isaac’s blessing, which had declared that nations and brothers would serve him (Genesis 27:29). The verb and noun come from the same root, ‘avad, “to serve.”

verses.bibleText: And so commanded he the second, and the third, and all that followed the droves, saying, On this manner shall ye speak unto Esau, when ye find him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And so commanded he the second, and the third, and all that followed the droves.” Each herdsman is given identical instructions. The repetition in the narrative mirrors the repetition on the road: Esau would hear the same words from the mouth of one servant after another. “On this manner shall ye speak unto Esau, when ye find him.”

The consistency served a purpose. A single message might be dismissed as flattery, but a message repeated with each new herd would show that Jacob’s humility was settled, not a passing tactic. Constancy in apology lends it credibility, and Jacob wanted Esau to have no doubt about his intentions.

From the first message to the last drove, Jacob calls himself Esau’s servant again and again (vv. 4, 18, 20). The steady repetition is the language of a man who has decided where he stands. He will not bargain for position; he will wait to be received.

wordNotes.term: הָעֲדָרִים (ha‘adarim) — the droves
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Eder is a flock or herd, a group of animals moving or pastured together. Jacob had watered Laban’s flocks at the well (Genesis 29:2-3), and later Migdal-eder, “tower of the flock,” marked a stage of his journey (Genesis 35:21). Micah takes up that place name in a messianic oracle (Micah 4:8).

verses.bibleText: And say ye moreover, Behold, thy servant Jacob is behind us. For he said, I will appease him with the present that goeth before me, and afterward I will see his face; peradventure he will accept of me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And say ye moreover, Behold, thy servant Jacob is behind us.” This line is repeated from verse 18 and placed last so that it would ring in Esau’s ears. Then the narrator lets us hear Jacob’s inner reasoning: “For he said, I will appease him with the present that goeth before me, and afterward I will see his face; peradventure he will accept of me.”

The sentence is built around the word “face,” which appears four times in the Hebrew. Literally Jacob says, “I will cover his face with the present that goes before my face, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will lift up my face.” To “cover the face” is to wipe away anger; to “lift the face” of someone is to receive him with favour and to forgive. Jacob hopes that the gift will remove the scowl from Esau’s face so that Esau will look on him kindly.

The verb “appease” is the word that elsewhere describes atonement. In the sanctuary it speaks of covering or wiping away sin so that the offender is reconciled to God (Leviticus 16:30). Here it is used between brothers. Jacob is seeking reconciliation with the one he has offended, and he knows that a wrong must be dealt with before fellowship can be restored. The language foreshadows the greater reconciliation that God would provide, in which the offended party himself supplies the covering, and the sinner is accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6).

The “peradventure” is honest. Jacob cannot be sure. Gifts can soften but cannot compel. Before he sees Esau’s face, he will see another face, and that encounter will settle what no present could. When the brothers meet, Jacob will tell Esau, “I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God” (33:10).

wordNotes.term: אֲכַפְּרָה פָנָיו (’akhapperah panav) — I will appease him
wordNotes.explanation: Kipper is the verb used throughout the Levitical system for making atonement (Leviticus 16:30). With “face” as its object, a combination found only here, it means to wipe the anger from someone’s face, to pacify. Proverbs 16:14 speaks of a wise man who will “pacify” a king’s wrath with the same verb. The religious overtones are clear: offence must be covered before acceptance is possible.

wordNotes.term: יִשָּׂא פָנָי (yissa’ panai) — he will accept of me
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “he will lift up my face,” an idiom for receiving someone with favour (Genesis 19:21; 1 Samuel 25:35). God uses it of accepting Job’s prayer for his friends (Job 42:8). The opposite is to let the face fall, the posture of rejection seen in Cain (Genesis 4:5-7).

verses.bibleText: So went the present over before him: and himself lodged that night in the company.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So went the present over before him.” The Hebrew says the gift “passed over upon his face,” continuing the play on “face” from the previous verse. Jacob’s gift goes ahead, bearing his apology in visible form.

“And himself lodged that night in the company.” The same verb “lodged” as in verse 13 closes the account of the gift. Jacob stays behind in the camp while his herds move off toward Esau. Everything humanly possible has been done: the messengers have been sent, the camp has been divided, the prayer has been offered, and the gift is on its way. Yet the night is still long, and Jacob cannot rest. In the next verse he rises again. The real business of the night has not yet begun.

wordNotes.term: וַתַּעֲבֹר הַמִּנְחָה עַל־פָּנָיו (vatta‘avor hamminchah ‘al-panav) — so went the present over before him
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Avar, “to pass over, cross,” runs through this section: the present passes over (v. 21), Jacob passes over the ford (v. 22), and he passes Penuel at dawn (v. 31). ‘Al-panav, “before his face,” keeps the word “face” in view, preparing for Peniel, “face of God” (v. 30), and for Jacob’s words to Esau in Genesis 33:10.

verses.bibleText: And he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons, and passed over the ford Jabbok.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he rose up that night.” Whatever rest Jacob had attempted was broken. In the darkness he gathers “his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons,” and brings them across “the ford Jabbok.” Dinah, his daughter, is not counted, since the narrative traces the line of the sons who would become the tribes. Benjamin is not yet born.

The Jabbok, today known as the Zarqa, flows westward through a deep gorge into the Jordan. Its fords were few, and crossing at night with women, small children, and livestock was hazardous. Why Jacob chose to move in the dark is not explained. Perhaps he wanted his family on the far side before Esau arrived; perhaps he could not bear to wait. The crossing places the household nearer to the land of promise and leaves Jacob himself behind on the northern bank.

The name Yabboq sounds like Ya‘aqov, Jacob, and like the verb vayye’aveq, “wrestled,” which appears in verse 24. The play on sounds signals that this river will be the scene of the decisive struggle of Jacob’s life. Later the Jabbok marked a boundary of Israel’s territory east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:24; Deuteronomy 3:16), but before it was a border on a map it was the place where Jacob became Israel.

wordNotes.term: מַעֲבַר יַבֹּק (ma‘avar Yabboq) — the ford Jabbok
wordNotes.explanation: Ma‘avar, “crossing place, ford,” comes from ‘avar, “to pass over.” Yabboq may derive from a root meaning “to flow” or “to empty out,” but in this chapter its sound matters most, echoing Ya‘aqov (Jacob) and ’avaq (wrestle). The river later formed the border between Sihon’s kingdom and the Ammonites (Numbers 21:24; Judges 11:13).

verses.bibleText: And he took them, and sent them over the brook, and sent over that he had.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he took them, and sent them over the brook, and sent over that he had.” The verse restates the crossing and makes it complete. Jacob ferries across not only his family but everything he owns. Nothing is left on his side of the stream except himself.

The stripping-away prepares for what follows. All the props of Jacob’s life, his wives, children, servants, herds, and wealth, are on the other bank. He cannot bargain with them, hide behind them, or lean on them. Whatever comes next, he will face it alone. God was about to meet Jacob without the possessions by which he had measured his success, so that he might discover what he was in himself, and what God would make of him.

Scripture often shows God’s servants going apart before a decisive moment: Moses on the mountain, Elijah alone at Horeb, and the Son of God himself, who went a little farther from his disciples to pray in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39). Solitude is where pretence falls away.

wordNotes.term: הַנָּחַל (hannachal) — the brook
wordNotes.explanation: Nachal is a wadi or stream valley, a watercourse that may flow all year or only in the rainy season. The Jabbok was a perennial nachal. The word is also used for the brook Kidron, which David crossed weeping in his flight (2 Samuel 15:23) and which Jesus crossed on the night of his betrayal (John 18:1).

verses.bibleText: And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob was left alone.” Everything he owned and everyone he loved had gone over the brook. He remained on the far bank in the dark, without servants to command or wealth to bargain with. What matters is the solitude. Jacob had always had something or someone to work with: a brother to outwit, a father to deceive, an uncle to outbargain. Now there was no one, and that was where God met him.

“And there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.” The attacker is introduced with the plainest word available, “a man.” He comes unannounced, and he takes the initiative; the verb has the man as its subject. In the darkness Jacob could not see who had seized him. With Esau’s threat hanging over him, he may well have supposed that an assassin or an advance raider had found him alone. He fought as a man fights for his life, and the struggle went on for hours.

The identity of this Man unfolds as the scene progresses. By the end Jacob calls the place Peniel because he has seen God face to face (v. 30). The prophet Hosea, recalling this night, says that Jacob “had power with God,” that “he had power over the angel, and prevailed,” and then names that Angel “the LORD God of hosts; the LORD is his memorial” (Hosea 12:3-5). The one who wrestled with Jacob was both a messenger and the LORD himself. That combination fits the Angel of the LORD who appeared to Hagar, who called to Abraham from heaven at Moriah, and who would later redeem Jacob “from all evil” (Genesis 16:13; 22:11-16; 48:16). The Wrestler at the Jabbok was the Son of God, appearing in human form before his incarnation, as he had come to Abraham at Mamre (18:1-2). The God who would one day take flesh permanently in Bethlehem first took on the form of a man to grapple with a frightened sinner in the dust.

The verb “wrestled” is rare, found only here and in the next verse. Its sound echoes both Jacob (Ya‘aqov) and the Jabbok (Yabboq), so that the man, the place, and the act are bound together by their very names.

The prophets later saw in this night a picture of the final distress of God’s people, “the time of Jacob’s trouble,” when they too will be shut up to God’s mercy and plead for deliverance (Jeremiah 30:7). As Jacob was delivered, so they will be. The struggle at the Jabbok reveals what God does with those he loves: he isolates them from every other support and then comes to them himself.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּאָבֵק (vayye’aveq) — and there wrestled
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ’avaq occurs only in Genesis 32:24-25. It is probably related to the noun ’avaq, “dust, fine powder” (Exodus 9:9; Isaiah 5:24), suggesting a struggle that rolls the combatants in the dust. Its consonants echo Ya‘aqov and Yabboq, linking the wrestler, the river, and the act. Hosea uses a different verb when he recalls the event, saying that Jacob “had power with God” (Hosea 12:3).

wordNotes.term: אִישׁ (’ish) — a man
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary word for a man or individual. Scripture uses it of heavenly visitors who appear in human form: the three men at Mamre (Genesis 18:2), the man who met Joshua as captain of the LORD’s host (Joshua 5:13-15), and the man clothed in linen in Daniel’s vision (Daniel 10:5). Here the plain word conceals a divine Person whose identity Jacob recognizes only gradually.

verses.bibleText: And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when he saw that he prevailed not against him.” The statement is startling. The Man could not overcome Jacob. The explanation lies in the nature of the contest. The divine Wrestler used only the strength of a man; he chose to meet Jacob on equal terms, limiting himself to what Jacob could resist. Jacob, for his part, had remarkable strength. He had once rolled the stone from a well single-handed (29:10), and twenty years of shepherding in heat and frost had hardened him (31:40). Through the night he held his own.

“He touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.” A single touch did what hours of grappling had not. The word “touched” is mild, the same verb used when the seraph touched Isaiah’s lips with a coal (Isaiah 6:7). With no visible effort the Man wrenched the socket of Jacob’s hip, the pivot of a wrestler’s strength. In that instant Jacob knew that his opponent was more than human. He could have ended the contest at any moment, and he had permitted it to go on so long only by his own restraint.

The touch was a severe mercy. It took away the one thing Jacob had always relied upon, his own ability to win. He could no longer fight; he could only hold on. The thigh in Hebrew thought is also associated with descendants (46:26; Exodus 1:5), and the blow fell at the very place from which the promised nation would come. The man who would father Israel would do so as one who had been broken by God.

The self-limitation of the divine Wrestler foreshadows the incarnation. In Christ, God humbled himself and took the form of a servant, contending with humanity on human terms (Philippians 2:6-8). He came close enough to be grappled with, and yet a single word from him could still the sea. At the Jabbok he showed Jacob both his condescension and his power.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגַּע בְּכַף־יְרֵכוֹ (vayyigga‘ bekhaf-yerekho) — he touched the hollow of his thigh
wordNotes.explanation: Naga‘, “to touch,” can describe a light contact or a decisive blow, depending on the context (Isaiah 6:7; Job 1:11). Kaf, “palm” or “hollow,” with yarekh, “thigh, hip,” describes the hip socket. Yarekh appears in oaths, when a servant places his hand under his master’s thigh (Genesis 24:2), and in phrases for descendants, “that came out of his loins” (Genesis 46:26).

verses.bibleText: And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh.” The Man now speaks for the first time. With dawn approaching, he asks to be released. Darkness had hidden his face, and daylight would reveal it. No sinful man could look upon the unveiled glory of God and live (Exodus 33:20), and the request to depart may have been a mercy to Jacob as much as anything else. The request also tests Jacob. Having been crippled, will he let go?

“And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.” The disabled man clings. He cannot wrestle any longer, but he can hold on, and he does so with all that remains of his strength. The touch and the voice have convinced him that he is grappling with no ordinary man, and he refuses to release the One who can give him what he most needs. At this point the struggle changes character. The fight with his hands becomes a plea with his lips.

Hosea tells us what that plea sounded like: “he wept, and made supplication unto him” (Hosea 12:4). Jacob’s victory was won with tears, not muscle. He had nothing to offer and no bargain to propose. All his life he had sought blessing by grasping, catching his brother’s heel, buying the birthright, disguising himself to take his father’s blessing. Now he asks for blessing as a gift from the only One who could grant it, and he asks as a man who knows that if this One leaves him unblessed, he has nothing.

The earlier Jacob also said, in effect, “bless me,” when he stood before blind Isaac (27:19). Then he hid his identity and took by deceit. Now he holds on in the open, broken, and asks. The difference between the two scenes is the difference between grasping and clinging. Grasping reaches for the gift and pushes the giver aside; clinging holds the giver and waits for the gift.

The principle runs through Scripture. Jesus told of a friend who knocked at midnight and a widow who would not stop pleading, and he taught that men ought always to pray and not to faint (Luke 11:5-8; 18:1-8). The Syrophoenician woman would not take silence for an answer (Matthew 15:22-28). Such persistence is no attempt to wear God down. It is the response of a heart that has learned it cannot live without him, and God honours it because he has awakened it.

wordNotes.term: לֹא אֲשַׁלֵּחֲךָ (lo’ ’ashallechakha) — I will not let thee go
wordNotes.explanation: Shalach in this intensive stem means to send away or release. The same form appears in the Man’s request, “Let me go.” Pharaoh’s refusal to “let my people go” uses it repeatedly (Exodus 5:1-2). The Bride in the Song uses a different verb with a similar resolve: “I held him, and would not let him go” (Song of Solomon 3:4).

wordNotes.term: כִּי אִם־בֵּרַכְתָּנִי (ki ’im-berakhtani) — except thou bless me
wordNotes.explanation: Ki ’im, “unless, except,” sets the condition. Barakh, “to bless,” is the key verb of the patriarchal story from Genesis 12:2-3 onward and of Jacob’s life in particular (Genesis 27:19, 34). The Man’s answer in verse 28 begins with the same ki ’im, translated “but,” so that the blessing answers the plea word for word.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, What is thy name? And he said, Jacob.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said unto him, What is thy name?” The Man knew the answer. The question was asked for Jacob’s sake. In the Bible a name often expresses a person’s character or history, and to speak one’s name is to own who one is. Twenty years earlier, when blind Isaac asked, “Who art thou, my son?” Jacob had answered with a lie: “I am Esau thy firstborn” (27:18-19). Now he is asked again, by One he cannot deceive.

“And he said, Jacob.” In a single word he confesses everything. Esau had spelled out what the name had come to mean: “Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times” (27:36). To say “Jacob” is to admit, “I am the heel-catcher, the one who takes what is not his.” No excuses are offered. The confession is complete because it is so bare.

This is the turning point of the scene. Blessing could not come while Jacob hid behind a borrowed identity. It comes when he tells the truth about himself. Scripture consistently joins confession and cleansing: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). David found that while he kept silence his bones wasted away, and when he acknowledged his sin the Lord forgave (Psalm 32:3-5). At the Jabbok, Jacob speaks his name, and God speaks a new one.

wordNotes.term: יַעֲקֹב (Ya‘aqov) — Jacob
wordNotes.explanation: The name was given because the infant came out holding Esau’s heel (‘aqev) (Genesis 25:26). The related verb ‘aqav means to follow at the heel, and so to overreach or supplant (Genesis 27:36; Jeremiah 9:4). Hosea recalls both the grasp in the womb and the wrestling at Peniel as two moments of one life (Hosea 12:3).

verses.bibleText: And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel.” Only one with authority over a person’s destiny could rename him. God had renamed Abram and Sarai (17:5, 15). This Man’s right to rename Jacob is a further hint of who he is. The old name had summed up Jacob’s past; the new one declares what God has made of him.

“For as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.” The KJV’s “as a prince hast thou power” renders a single Hebrew verb meaning “you have striven” or “you have contended.” Israel is formed from that verb and the name of God, and in this setting the Man himself explains it: Jacob has striven with God and has prevailed. Jacob prevailed, and yet the One who prevailed over Jacob was God.

How did Jacob prevail? He did not throw his opponent; he was crippled in a moment. He prevailed by holding on in his weakness and pleading for a blessing that only God could give. Hosea’s commentary is decisive: “he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him” (Hosea 12:4). The victory was the victory of faith, of a man who could no longer help himself and so cast himself wholly on God. Paul learned the same paradox: “when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). God allowed himself to be overcome by the prayer of a broken man, for that was the very surrender he had been working toward all night.

“And with men.” Jacob had contended with Esau from the womb, with Isaac in the tent, and with Laban for twenty years. In each contest he had prevailed by cunning. Now his strivings are reframed. The decisive struggle was always with God, and having prevailed there by surrender, he need not fear the struggle with Esau that awaits him in the morning.

The new name marked a change of character, from deceiver to one who prevails with God. Yet Scripture continues to call him Jacob as well as Israel, unlike Abraham, who was never again called Abram. The transformation was real, and it would also be worked out through the rest of a life that still knew failure and grief. In time the name passed to his descendants, the nation of Israel, and Paul applies it to all who share Jacob’s faith: “they are not all Israel, which are of Israel” (Romans 9:6). Every believer who has been brought to the end of himself and has clung to Christ receives a new name (Revelation 2:17; 3:12).

wordNotes.term: יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisra’el) — Israel
wordNotes.explanation: Formed from the verb sarah, “to strive, contend, persist,” and ’El, “God.” Grammatically the name could mean “God strives” or “may God contend,” but the explanation given in the verse ties it to Jacob’s striving with God and prevailing. The renaming is confirmed at Bethel (Genesis 35:10). Outside this chapter the verb appears only in Hosea 12:3-4, where the prophet recalls this night.

wordNotes.term: שָׂרִיתָ ... וַתּוּכָל (sarita ... vattukhal) — thou hast power ... and hast prevailed
wordNotes.explanation: Sarita is “you have striven” from sarah; the KJV’s “as a prince” reflects an older link with sar, “prince.” Yakhol means to be able, to overcome, and is used of prevailing in conflict (Genesis 30:8; Numbers 22:6). Hosea repeats both verbs: Jacob “had power over the angel, and prevailed” (Hosea 12:4), and then adds that he wept and made supplication, revealing how the victory was won.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob asked him, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, thy name. And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name? And he blessed him there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob asked him, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, thy name.” Jacob has given his name; now he asks for the Man’s. The request is natural, and courteously put. In the ancient world, to know a being’s name was thought to give some hold over it, and pagan religion often tried to use divine names as tools of power. Jacob may have wanted only certainty about the One who had blessed him, but the question still reaches for a kind of mastery that God does not grant.

“And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name?” The question answers the question. It invites Jacob to consider what he already knows. The touch that crippled him, the power to rename him, the authority to bless: these have already told him who his opponent is. When Manoah asked the Angel of the LORD for his name, he received a similar reply, with the added word that the name was “secret,” that is, wonderful, beyond comprehension (Judges 13:17-18). Isaiah uses the same word, “Wonderful,” for the child who would be called “The mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6).

The Man withholds his name, yet he does not withhold himself. “And he blessed him there.” Jacob received what he had asked for in verse 26. The blessing was given at that spot, at that moment, before the Man departed. The fuller revelation of the divine name would come later, to Moses at the burning bush and on Sinai (Exodus 3:13-15; 34:5-7), and supremely in Christ, who made the Father’s name known (John 17:6). For Jacob the blessing had to suffice, and it did.

wordNotes.term: לָמָּה זֶּה תִּשְׁאַל לִשְׁמִי (lammah zeh tish’al lishmi) — wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name?
wordNotes.explanation: The same words appear in Judges 13:18, where the Angel of the LORD replies to Manoah and adds that his name is pil’i, “wonderful,” beyond human grasp. The related noun pele’ names the coming Child in Isaiah 9:6. In both scenes the visitor’s refusal is itself a disclosure: the one asking is in the presence of God.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel.” He had named Bethel, “house of God,” after his dream (28:19), and Mahanaim, “two camps,” after the angels (v. 2). Now he names the riverbank Peniel, “face of God.” The Man would not tell his name, so Jacob names the place, testifying to what he has learned there.

“For I have seen God face to face.” Jacob now says plainly what the Man’s reply implied. His opponent was God. “Face to face” describes immediate, personal encounter. Scripture uses it of God speaking with Moses (Exodus 33:11; Deuteronomy 34:10) and of God speaking with Israel at Sinai (Deuteronomy 5:4). It does not mean that Jacob beheld the unveiled glory of the divine being, which no man can see and live (Exodus 33:20; John 1:18). He met God veiled in human form, the form the Son would one day take permanently. In Jesus, the face of God was finally shown to men: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (John 14:9).

“And my life is preserved.” Jacob had expected death from his brother, and instead he had met God and lived. The verb is the one he used in his prayer: “Deliver me” (v. 11). God answered that plea at Peniel before he answered it at Esau’s side. Gideon and Manoah later feared they would die because they had seen the Angel of the LORD (Judges 6:22-23; 13:22), and Isaiah cried “Woe is me” when he saw the King (Isaiah 6:5). Each was spared because God came near in mercy.

The word translated “life” is nephesh, which here means Jacob himself, the living person whose life had been in danger. Jacob does not speak of an inner soul surviving apart from the body; he rejoices that he, a mortal man, is still alive after meeting the living God. His survival is all of grace, and he knows it.

wordNotes.term: פְּנִיאֵל (Peni’el) — Peniel
wordNotes.explanation: “Face of God,” from panim, “face,” and ’El, “God.” Verse 31 uses the variant Penuel, the form found in later history, where Gideon tore down its tower (Judges 8:8-9, 17) and Jeroboam fortified it (1 Kings 12:25). The name fixes in geography the testimony of Jacob’s night.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּנָּצֵל נַפְשִׁי (vattinnatsel nafshi) — and my life is preserved
wordNotes.explanation: Nitsal is the passive of natsal, “to snatch away, deliver,” the verb of Jacob’s plea in verse 11. Nephesh denotes the living person, his life or self (Genesis 2:7; 19:19-20). The clause means “I have been rescued, I am still alive.” The phrase “face to face” that precedes it, panim ’el-panim, is the one used when the LORD spoke with Moses at the tabernacle door (Exodus 33:11).

verses.bibleText: And as he passed over Penuel the sun rose upon him, and he halted upon his thigh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And as he passed over Penuel the sun rose upon him.” The image is full of meaning. Twenty years earlier, as Jacob fled from home, “the sun was set” when he lay down at Bethel (28:11). The years of exile began at sunset and now end at sunrise. The long night of fear, guilt, and hard service is over. Jacob crosses the stream toward his waiting family and the land of promise as a new day breaks over him. Malachi would later speak of “the Sun of righteousness” arising “with healing in his wings” for those who fear God’s name (Malachi 4:2).

“And he halted upon his thigh.” The same sunrise that marks his blessing also shows his limp. Jacob walks away from Peniel crippled, and the injury appears to have stayed with him. Every step reminds him of the night when God touched him. His natural strength had been broken, but in its place he had learned to lean on God. The limp is the mark of a man who has prevailed through weakness, and it goes with him into the meeting with Esau.

Paul carried his own reminder, a thorn in the flesh that kept him dependent on Christ’s grace (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). Those who pass through their own Peniel often bear some lasting mark of the struggle. The risen Christ himself still bears the wounds of his conflict for us (John 20:27). Yet the scars of the redeemed will not last forever. The prophets promise that the Lord will gather “her that halteth” and make the lame a remnant and a strong nation (Micah 4:6-7), and in the new earth “shall the lame man leap as an hart” (Isaiah 35:6).

wordNotes.term: צֹלֵעַ (tsolea‘) — he halted
wordNotes.explanation: A participle from tsala‘, “to limp,” describing continuing action: he was limping. The verb is rare. Its other occurrences are in prophetic promises that God will gather and save the lame, the scattered remnant of his people (Micah 4:6-7; Zephaniah 3:19). The limping patriarch becomes a picture of the weak remnant whom God restores.

verses.bibleText: Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day: because he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh in the sinew that shrank.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day.” The narrator steps outside the story to connect it to a custom known in his own time. Jacob’s descendants, now called “the children of Israel” for the first time in Scripture, refrained from eating this part of an animal in memory of their ancestor’s injury.

The custom is not part of the law given at Sinai, and it is not mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament. It grew up as a family and national memorial, in the same way that place names such as Bethel, Mahanaim, and Peniel kept the memory of God’s dealings alive. Every time an animal was prepared for food, the people would be reminded of the night when God touched Jacob and gave him the name they bore. The exact identification of “the sinew which shrank” is uncertain; it is usually understood as the sciatic nerve, which runs along the hip.

“Because he touched the hollow of Jacob’s thigh in the sinew that shrank.” The verse ends by repeating the cause. The nation of Israel owed its name to a night when its father was crippled and blessed in the same encounter. To remember the sinew was to remember that Israel began with a man who could only cling to God. The people of God in every age carry a similar memory. The Lord’s Supper calls believers to remember the body of Christ broken for them (1 Corinthians 11:24), the deeper wounding by which their own new name was secured.

wordNotes.term: גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה (gid hannasheh) — the sinew which shrank
wordNotes.explanation: Gid means sinew or tendon (Job 10:11; Ezekiel 37:6). The meaning of nasheh is uncertain. The KJV’s “which shrank” follows the Greek Old Testament, which took it to mean “numbed” or “withered.” Later Jewish practice identified it as the sciatic nerve and its branches. Whatever the precise anatomy, the phrase marks the place of Jacob’s injury.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When a wrong from your past finally catches up with you, where do you turn first?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God meets Jacob’s fear with angels, answers his prayer with a night of wrestling, and blesses him only when his own strength is broken, so that the deceiver becomes Israel, prevailing by clinging to God.
discussionQuestions: What did the angels at Mahanaim tell Jacob about his situation that his eyes alone could not?
Which features of Jacob’s prayer in verses 9-12 can shape our own prayers in a crisis?
Were Jacob’s gifts to Esau an act of unbelief, or a fitting attempt to make amends alongside prayer?
Why did the Wrestler cripple Jacob before blessing him, and what does Hosea 12:4 add to our understanding of the struggle?
What does it mean that Jacob “prevailed” after he could no longer fight?
commonMisunderstandings: The Wrestler was not a demon, a river spirit, or Esau’s guardian angel; Jacob calls him God, and Hosea calls him both the Angel and the LORD God of hosts.
Jacob did not win the blessing by physical strength or persistence as a kind of merit; he received it when, disabled, he could only hold on and ask.
The new name did not mean Jacob never stumbled again; it marked a turning point in his relationship with God that the rest of his life would work out.
Seeing God “face to face” does not mean Jacob beheld the unveiled glory of God; he met God in a human form that veiled that glory.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Let the chapter move from fear to prayer to surrender. Jacob’s planning is not condemned, but it cannot settle his deepest problem, which is his standing with God; the night at the Jabbok deals with that first, and the meeting with Esau follows.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The same Lord who wrestled with Jacob comes to every one who is still trying to secure the blessing by his own devices. Stop striving, take hold of him in your weakness, confess who you are, and let him give you a new name.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Conversion and assurance: God brings the self-reliant sinner to the end of his own strength so that, confessing his sin and clinging to Christ, he receives forgiveness, a new character, and a new name.
flow: Jacob’s past sin had followed him for twenty years, and he could not undo it.
He prayed, confessing that he was unworthy of the least of God’s mercies, and pleaded God’s promises.
In the night the pre-incarnate Christ met him, and one touch ended his reliance on his own strength.
Clinging in weakness, Jacob confessed his name and nature, and received the new name Israel.
Christ still meets sinners who will hold to him, forgives them, and makes them new.
simpleIllustrations: A swimmer who fights the lifeguard can drown them both; rescue begins when he stops struggling and holds on to the one who came for him.
A man who signs papers under a new name after a court has cleared him does so because the verdict has changed his standing, not because he invented a new identity.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you, like Jacob, stop relying on your own schemes, confess your sin, and hold on to Christ until you know that he has blessed you?
cautions: Do not present persistence in prayer as a means of forcing God’s hand; Jacob prevailed because God chose to be held and to bless.
Do not suggest that conversion removes every scar or weakness at once; Jacob limped for the rest of his life.
Treat the identity of the Wrestler with reverence, drawing it from Hosea 12 and Jacob’s own words rather than speculation.

reflectionQuestions: Am I aware that God’s unseen hosts surround me on the road he has called me to walk?
Is there a brother or sister I have wronged, to whom I need to take the first humble step?
When I pray, do I plead God’s promises and confess my unworthiness, or do I bargain?
Where is God touching my strength so that I will learn to cling to him?
What old name, what pattern of self-reliance, do I need to confess so that God can give me a new one?
